newsitem.title: USA: Trees, power lines fly as Fran strikes N. Carolina.
newsitem.headline: Trees, power lines fly as Fran strikes N. Carolina.

text.p: Hurricane Fran pounded the North Carolina coast late on Thursday with wind gusts of more than 120 mph (193 kmh) that ripped down telephone lines, overturned cars and blew up electricity transformers.
The storm dumped heavy rain of more than six inches (15 cms) on already rain-swollen rivers, raising fears of flooding throughout much of North Carolina, officials said.
An elderly motorist died on a rain-slicked South Carolina highway on Thursday afternoon when she lost control of her car and crashed into a tree, the state highway patrol said.
At 8 p.m. EDT (2400 GMT), the eye of the hurricane moved ashore near Cape Fear, North Carolina, with sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kmh) and even stronger gusts.
"It's pretty rough out here," said Beth Howell, a Wilmington resident who called WECT-TV, the local NBC affiliate, to report the damage in her neighbourhood.

"The wind blew a tree over on the roof and it knocked the chimney in, so we've got bricks coming down the fireplace and the wind is blowing through the bottom," Howell added. "It's really wild outside."

Fran followed a path similar to that of Hurricane Bertha in July. Bertha damaged 1,400 homes and 250 businesses in the Wilmington area, causing $22 million in damage, according to preliminary insurance estimates.

Along the coast of North and South Carolina, nuclear power reactors were shut, shops and bridges closed and homes boarded up as people waited out the storm. Some 200,000 residents evacuated low-lying areas and checked into motels, stayed with friends or went to Red Cross shelters.
One resident of Carolina Beach, an evacuated area, said she remained in her home to take care of her pets.

"Except for the water getting awfully deep, it's not bad here. There's about three feet of water around us," Donna Ludlow told WECT-TV. "In case my sister is listening, we're fine. But her property is underwater."

In Wilmington, North Carolina, emergency officials said they expected the entire city to lose power. Several electricity transformers lit up the night sky when they exploded in bursts of orange light that crackled loudly.
Wilmington, founded in 1739, has 60,000 residents, a major port and picturesque Victorian homes that are the foundation of a thriving tourist industry.

Residents of Charleston, an historic port city battered seven years ago by Hurricane Hugo, breathed a sigh of relief as forecasters said Fran's course would put the eye of the storm more than 100 miles (160 km) to the north.
Hurricane forecasters were also keeping a close eye on the season's eighth tropical depression far out in the Atlantic.
The National Hurricane Centre said the depression was 535 miles (860 km) east of the Leeward Islands and was expected to strengthen into Tropical Storm Hortense by late Friday.
